resources.string: How the cerebral cortex guides a reach
One example of a normal voluntary reach. The regions can work together as the reach unfolds; the chapters and paths do not show a fixed processing order or exact nerve routes.

On the outer surface of the left hemisphere, the primary motor cortex lies just in front of the central sulcus and the primary somatosensory cortex just behind it. Both help guide the right hand in this example.

As the fingertip rests on a surface, skin receptors signal contact. Signals from muscles and joints also report the position of the arm. The primary somatosensory cortex processes both kinds of information.
Plan a reach toward the cup
The posterior parietal and premotor regions work together, using the position of the hand and the location of the cup to help plan the reach.
The primary motor cortex helps send commands down to the spinal cord. Spinal motor neurons activate muscles at the shoulder and elbow, moving the hand toward the cup.
Keep sensing as the hand moves
While the arm moves, fresh information about its position keeps arriving. The brain can use it to update outgoing commands. When the fingertip meets the cup, touch signals report contact again.
